title: {{NAME}} and the Princess of the Prehistoric Park
moral: Leadership means understanding what everything in your care needs, even if it is very large.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a deep forest green jacket with gold buttons, tan riding trousers, and high riding boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
Princess Elara had inherited the Royal Natural History Park at the age of nine and immediately made three decisions.

One: no more hunting, ever. Two: the park needed a proper veterinarian. Three: the Tyrannosaurus in the east paddock needed a name and it was going to be Gerald.

She hired {{NAME}} as junior keeper. His first day: the rabbits in the west meadow had chewed through the fence separating them from the Triceratops enclosure.

"Is that a problem?" he asked.

"Gerald thinks so," said the princess. "Gerald doesn't like surprises."

pages.content:
Gerald, it turned out, had very specific preferences.

He liked the east paddock. He liked eating at dawn and dusk. He liked being observed from a respectful distance. He did not like: rabbits in his peripheral vision, loud noises before breakfast, or the junior keeper forgetting to bring his morning enrichment item.

{{NAME}} kept a notebook. Gerald's preferences took up six pages by the end of the first week.

"He's like a very large cat," {{NAME}} told the princess.

"Don't let him hear you say that," she said seriously.

pages.content:
The crisis came when three young deer wandered into Gerald's paddock through a drainage gap and couldn't find their way out.

Gerald was awake. Gerald was also, clearly, confused rather than aggressive: the deer were too small to be interesting and too numerous to ignore.

{{NAME}} went in through the maintenance gate while Princess Elara created a distraction with Gerald's favourite enrichment object from outside.

Five minutes. Three deer retrieved. Gerald: still watching, now holding his enrichment object, looking somewhat satisfied.

pages.content:
By the end of the first month, {{NAME}} had mapped every animal's routine, needs, and personality.

The Triceratops liked being brushed. Gerald liked puzzles. The deer preferred not to be herded. The rabbits went wherever they liked regardless of fencing.

"You know all of them," said Princess Elara.

"That's the job," said {{NAME}}.

"Most keepers know the animals. You seem to know what they're thinking."

He looked out at Gerald, who was currently staring at a butterfly with great concentration.

"Some of them are easier to read than others," he said.

pages.content:
On his way home each evening, {{NAME}} always stopped at Gerald's fence and said goodnight.

Gerald always watched him from the middle of the paddock, utterly still, until {{NAME}} was out of sight.

He found this comforting rather than ominous, which said something about how the first month had gone.

In bed that night, he looked up at the ceiling and thought about the deer rescued from the paddock, the rabbits causing manageable chaos, the princess writing policy changes in her royal notebook.

He fell asleep to the imagined sound of a very large creature settling in for the night.
